newsitem.title: KENYA: UN environment agency, Kenya sign satellite deal.
newsitem.headline: UN environment agency, Kenya sign satellite deal.

text.p: The U.N. environment agency and Kenya on Friday signed a long-delayed agreement that will pave the way for a new advanced satellite telecommunications system to cut costs and improve the agency's information network.
The deal was signed by Kenya's Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka and the executive director of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP), Elizabeth Dowdeswell, at Musyoka's office.

The signing came four days after officials attending UNEP's Governing Council meeting in Nairobi -- the agency's legislative and top policy organ -- complained that Kenya was frustrating UNEP efforts to cut costs by refusing to authorise the deal.
The Council first approved the deal in 1995 but Kenya, where UNEP's global headquarters is based, showed no sign of quickly authorising the satellite system.

"The advanced capability made possible through this system will better equip UNEP to fulfil its leadership role in providing up-to-date, easily accessible, well-organised information and scientific data to the rest of the world via the global information highways," Dowdeswell said.
She said six European nations -- Austria, Belgium, Norway, Spain, Switzerland and Britain -- provided the initial funding for the satellite system.
Dowdeswell said the new system will provide guaranteed delivery and access to environmental data without congestion.
Experts at the Governing Council meeting -- attended by ministers and representatives from 100 nations -- said the satellite system would cut UNEP's communications bill by half.

Officials said Kenya was initially reluctant to sign the satellite deal because of fears it would hit state-owned Kenya Posts and Telecommunications Corporation (KPTC), which receives $5 million annually from UNEP for phone bills.
UNEP is reeling from financial woes caused by unpaid dues from Western donors demanding reform and cost-saving measures.
Key donors such as Japan, the United States, Britain, France and Italy are reluctant to pay, arguing UNEP has become less effective since the 1992 Earth summit.
As a result UNEP has seen its budget drop sharply over the last few years as donors link funding to reforms in the agency.
